title: N-terminal domain swapping: A new paradigm for spermidine/spermine N -acetyltransferase (SSAT) protein structures?

sections.abstract: Enterococcus faecalis is a multi-drug-resistant human pathogen that is found in a variety of environments and is challenging to treat. Under stress conditions, some bacteria regulate intracellular polyamine concentrations via polyamine acetyltransferases to reduce their toxicity. The E. faecalis genome encodes two polyamine acetyltransferases: PmvE and BltD. Both of these proteins belong to the Gcn5-related N -acetyltransferase (GNAT) superfamily. It is unclear why there are two enzymes with similar substrate specificities in this organism. To better understand the structure/function relationship of the E. faecalis BltD enzyme, we determined its crystal structure and performed additional assays to explore its oligomeric state and enzymatic activity. The goal was to determine whether there were structural or catalytic differences between this enzyme and other polyamine acetyltransferases that could explain this redundancy and be exploited for future development of targeted inhibitors for this important human pathogen. We found the BltD enzyme was structurally unique due to its N-terminal domain swapped dimer. However, this enzyme adopts a catalytically active monomer rather than dimer in solution. This indicates the crystal structure we obtained may represent a state that forms at high protein and salt concentrations and at low pH used during crystallization. The BltD dimer found in the crystal may represent a unique view of how an inhibitory peptide or molecule could be designed to occupy its active site. Additionally, this structure shows the extensive flexibility of the N-terminal portion of the E. faecalis BltD enzyme.
sections.introduction:
Gram-positive Enterococcal bacteria are ubiquitous in nature and can be found in a variety of environments, including water, soil, plants, and gut microbiomes of many mammalian and avian species; reviewed in Ref. [ 1 ]. Their ability to colonize different environments is largely due to their robustness in surviving different temperatures, salts, nutrients, disinfectants, and pH ranges [ 2 ]. While Enterococcal species can be innocuous, some species, such as Enterococcus faecalis and E. faecium , are opportunistic pathogens that have developed multi-drug resistance to all classes of clinically available antibiotics. This makes them particularly challenging to treat and poses a significant threat to human health [ 3 ]. One route bacteria use to survive harsh conditions, including antibiotic treatment and colonization of the gut, is the formation of biofilms. It is becoming increasingly clear that biofilms can also be used as reservoirs for easily exchanging genetic material between organisms during stress conditions, especially for Enterococcal species [ 4 ].

In some bacteria, biofilms are regulated by polyamines and can be critical for growth, including many Gram-negative bacteria and some Gram-positive bacteria like Bacillus subtilis [ 5 – 7 ]. However, not all bacteria follow this paradigm. For example, growth and biofilm formation of Gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and E. faecalis are polyamine-independent, where polyamines neither enhance nor prohibit biofilm formation in either bacterium [ 8 ]. Polyamines, which are also called growth factors in older literature, are important cationic molecules that are either inherently produced within an organism through biosynthetic routes or as degradative products of amino acids [ 9 , 10 ]. They can also be acquired extracellularly via polyamine uptake transporters [ 11 , 12 ]. While these molecules are found across all domains of life, many bacterial species and some eukaryotic parasites lack the biosynthetic machinery to produce polyamines [ 9 ]. In fact, many Gram-positive bacterial species, including S. aureus, Lactobacillus casei , and E. faecalis , do not produce polyamines intracellularly [ 13 ]. Despite this, the growth of some lactic acid bacteria is stimulated by spermidine or spermine, but many others, including E. faecalis , are not [ 14 ]. It has also been shown that E. faecalis strains O1GRF and V583 do not accumulate spermidine when grown in polyamine-free media [ 8 ], but many lactic acid bacteria, including E. faecalis , can import spermine and spermidine when grown in polyamine-supplemented media [ 14 ].

Acetylation plays an important role in maintaining the intracellular concentrations of polyamines within bacteria. It is thought that E. faecalis imports polyamines to aid survival under various stress conditions, though the exact role(s) of polyamines and their regulation within this organism remain unclear. The E. faecalis genome encodes two polyamine acetyltransferases that acetylate polyamines: 1) PmvE ( p olyamine m etabolism and v irulence of E . faecalis , gene ef_3001 ) ( Ef PmvE) [ 15 ], and 2) BltD ( B mr- l ike t ransporter d ownstream, gene ef_1086 ) ( Ef BltD) [ 8 ]. The pmvE gene is an essential gene in E. faecalis and it is located downstream from the slyA gene, which is a regulator that negatively controls pmvE transcription and is important for E. faecalis persistence, virulence, and bile salt stress [ 16 , 17 ]. The Ef PmvE protein was identified as a virulence factor and is also important for its persistence in macrophages [ 15 ]. It has been shown to acetylate the polyamines putrescine and spermine, and it is a homolog of the previously characterized Bacillus subtilis PaiA enzyme [ 15 ]. The Ef BltD enzyme appears to adopt a traditional role of acetylating polyamines with a preference for spermine over spermidine [ 8 ]. However, less is known about the E. faecalis BltD protein than from its namesake from B. subtilis . For example, the operons that contain the bltD genes are not consistent between these two organisms; blt and bltD are co-transcribed in B. subtilis [ 18 ], but to our knowledge a blt homolog is not present on the same operon as bltD in E. faecalis . Additionally, B. subtilis blt gene expression was found to be environmentally dependent upon acrA (acriflavine resistance mutation) [ 18 ], and overexpression of BltD only occurred when acrA was mutated [ 19 ]. However, it has been shown that when the B. subtilis BltD protein is expressed, it acetylates spermidine at the N 1 -position (not N 8 ) [ 19 ]. Additionally, the B. subtilis BltD enzyme exhibits a preference for acetylating spermine over spermidine and its substrate binding mechanism is random [ 20 ]. Similar enzyme kinetics have been shown for Ef BltD [ 8 ].

The Ef BltD enzyme was previously selected as a target for structural studies during the early stages of the structural genomics efforts within the Midwest Center for Structural Genomics (MCSG) and the Protein Structure Initiative (PSI) with the aim to crystallize proteins with unique structural folds. The Ef BltD protein structure was deposited into the Protein Data Bank (PDB) in 2006 in its apo form (PDB ID: 2fl4), but no further characterizations were performed. At the time, it was unclear to us that this structure was a homolog of the previously characterized BltD spermidine/spermine N -acetyltransferase from B . subtilis until recent advancements within the UniProt database that improved the association of 3D crystal structures with specific genes. Due to our interest in determining 3D structures of polyamine acetyltransferases in complex with substrates that we and others functionally determined, we resurrected this project for further crystallization trials in 2021 in collaboration with the CSGID/CSBID (Center for Structural Genomics of Infectious Diseases/Center for Structural Biology of Infectious Diseases). Additionally, we used this project as a tool for training San Francisco State University (SFSU) undergraduate and Masters students to crystallize proteins at Argonne National Laboratory, kinetically characterize the enzymes at SFSU, and analyze the 3D structures and write manuscripts for publication within a Masters-level lecture course at SFSU during the Fall 2023 semester.
sections.methods:
The EF1086 gene was amplified from the genomic DNA of a vancomycin-resistant clinical isolate E. faecalis V583 [ 21 ] (locus tag Ef_1086 , NCBI Accession AAO80887.1 , UniProt ID: Q836M4 ) and subcloned into the ampicillin resistant pMCSG53 vector using ligation independent cloning using previously described procedures [ 22 ]. The N-terminus contains the sequence MHHHHHHENLYFQSNA, which encodes a polyhistidine tag and Tobacco Etch Virus (TEV) protease cleavage site; after tag removal the residues SNA remain at the N-terminus of the protein. The Ef BltD protein is comprised of 151 amino acids, with a molecular weight of 17.7 kDa and theoretical pI of 5.07 in absence of the tag but presence of SNA residues. BL21 Gold DE3 cells were transformed with the plasmid and were grown, expressed, and harvested as described previously [ 23 ]; a total culture volume of 1 L of LB media was used. Briefly, cells were resuspended in 25 mL of buffer A (50 mM Hepes pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 5 % glycerol, 10 mM β-mercaptoethanol (BME), 20 mM imidazole) and frozen at −80 °C.

Crude extracts were thawed and sonicated in the presence of one protease inhibitor tablet (Complete Protease Inhibitor Cocktail Roche) and centrifuged as described previously [ 23 ]. Cleared lysate was then syringe filtered (0.45 μM polyvinylidine difluoride (PVDF)) and loaded onto a 5 mL HisTrap HP nickel-affinity chromatography column (Cytiva) in buffer A. Non-specifically bound protein was washed from the column in buffer A and eluted in buffer B (buffer A with 250 mM imidazole). The protein yield at this step was 26 mg of pure protein, which was subjected to TEV protease cleavage using a ratio of 1:30 TEV protease to protein. The cleavage reaction was allowed to proceed at RT for 1 h and then moved to 4 °C overnight. The TEV protease was previously cloned into the pRK603 expression vector [ 24 ] and protein was purified as described above except it was buffer exchanged and stored at 10 mg/mL in 50 mM Tris pH 7.5, 1 mM EDTA, 5 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), and 25% glycerol. The following day the Ef BltD cleaved protein was purified in buffer A, buffer exchanged into crystallization buffer (10 mM Tris HCl pH 8.3, 500 mM NaCl, 5 mM BME) and concentrated using Amicon 10 kDa MWCO centrifugation devices. Protein purity was assessed by SDS-PAGE and found to be purified to near homogeneity ( Supplemental Fig. 1 ).

The Ef BltD protein was subjected to sitting-drop vapor diffusion crystallization trials using protein (9.1 mg/mL in crystallization buffer) in the presence or absence of donor or acceptor substrates (4 mM spermine, spermidine, AcCoA, or CoA). Protein was added in a 1:1 ratio with reservoir solution (0.4 μL total volume) in the drop with 135 μL of solution in the reservoir in Greiner Bio-One CrystalQuick round well (3 wells per reservoir), concave bottom, low birefringence 96-well plates. Crystallization screens that were tested included Index and Salt Rx (Hampton Research), ComPAS (NeXtal Biotechnologies), Classics II (Jena Bioscience), and MCSG-3 and Top-96 screens (Anatrace). Suitable crystals grew in absence of substrates in the Index screen well A8 (0.1 M sodium acetate trihydrate pH 4.5, 3 M NaCl) and were harvested and cryoprotected in a reservoir solution supplemented with saturated sucrose before flash cooled in liquid nitrogen. The structure of the Ef BltD protein that was previously deposited into the PDB (PDB ID: 2fl4) crystallized in the same condition.

X-ray diffraction experiments were conducted at 100 K at the BL 9–2 beamline at Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL) remotely using a PILATUS3 6M detector (Dectris). Conditions at SSRL included a 50 × 50 mm X-ray beam, with 10 % transmission, 1.0 deg/0.5 s exposure and 250 mm crystal to detector distance. For highly redundant data, 360 degrees of continuous rotation at wavelength 0.9795 Å were collected. The crystal used for data collection diffracted to 1.50 Å resolution. Data were processed and scaled using HKL3000 [ 25 ] and the highest resolution data were cut based on I/σ (1.00), completeness (70 %), and CC 1/2 (0.4). The crystal belongs to space group P3 (see Table 1 for more details). The structure was determined by molecular replacement using Molrep [ 26 ] and an AlphaFold2 [ 27 ] model was generated and used as the search model, followed by brief rigid body refinement and initial refinement in Refmac5.5 [ 28 ], which were all implemented in HKL3000. The asymmetric unit of the P3 unit cell contains a dimer. The structure was refined by iterative refinement cycles with manual adjustment using Coot plus restrained refinement using Phenix (phenix.refine) [ 29 ] and Refmac5.5 until the structures converged to the model with reasonable stereochemistry and R work /R free parameters. As the crystal was twined, phenix.refine and Refmac5.5 were alternated to better refine the twined crystal structure in the final few rounds of refinement. The progress of the refinement was carefully monitored with R work and R free values, which were calculated by using 5 % of reflections randomly selected from the total unique reflections and these 5 % of data were excluded from all refinement. After each refinement cycle, the refined structure was checked with Molprobity [ 30 ] and Procheck/Ramachandran plot [ 31 ]. The final structure contains two protein chains A and B with residues 0–146 and 0–145 (where zero represents A from the remaining amino acids (SNA) at the N-terminus after cleavage), respectively in addition to one acetic acid, 160 water molecules, and nine chloride and sodium ions. Statistics for all crystal diffraction data collection, processing and structure refinement is shown in Table 1 . The final refined structure was validated with PDB validation before deposition with PDB ID 9dsb.

The Ef BltD protein was subjected to analytical size exclusion chromatography (SEC) at 12 °C using a Thermo Scientific Dionex ICS-5000+ system with PDA detector and autosampler. The protein was injected (20 μL of 7 mg/mL protein) onto an SEC column (SRT SEC-150 5 μm 150 Å 7.8 × 250 mm; Sepax Technologies) that was equilibrated with buffer (50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl) at a flow rate of 1 mL/min. We also performed this experiment to partially mimic crystallization conditions by dialyzing the protein into 50 mM sodium acetate pH 4.5 and 1 M NaCl for 3.5 h in a 0.5 mL 10 kDa MWCO dialysis cassette and then concentrating by centrifugation as described above. No precipitation was observed. Additional Ef BltD protein samples in the presence of 1 mM or 5 mM AcCoA, 1 mM spermine, or 5 mM AcCoA and 8 mM spermine were also prepared and injected to determine if protein retention times were affected in the presence/absence of donor or acceptor substrates in Tris pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl. Protein molecular weight standards from low and high molecular weight gel filtration calibration kits (Cytiva) were injected onto the column in both buffers and their retention times were used to estimate the molecular weight of the Ef BltD protein in presence and absence of ligands at pH 8.0. The mixture of protein standards included ferritin (440 kDa), aldolase (158 kDa), conalbumin (75 kDa), ovalbumin (44 kDa), carbonic anhydrase (29 kDa), and ribonuclease A (13.7 kDa). Retention times of protein standards were used to generate a plot of log M r vs K av and the slope and y-intercept of this line was used to calculate M r of the protein based on its retention time.

The Ef BltD protein was buffer exchanged into 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 500 mM NaCl and then diluted to 1 mg/mL for enzyme assays. Different dilutions of enzyme were screened for activity toward spermine, spermidine, thialysine, l -lysine, tobramycin, and kanamycin B (reaction contained 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM acceptor substrate and 1 mM AcCoA) to determine the optimal concentration of enzyme for steady-state kinetic characterization. Spermine and spermidine substrate saturation curves (0–1 mM) were produced in a reaction volume of 50 μL with 1 mM AcCoA using 20 nM and 1 μM of enzyme for spermine and spermidine curves, respectively. AcCoA substrate saturation curves (0–1 mM) were produced in the presence of 1 mM spermine and 20 nM of enzyme. Reactions proceeded for 10 min at 37 °C in 50 mM Tris pH 8.0, 100 mM NaCl and were initiated with 10 μL of enzyme. The solution used to stop the reactions was altered from prior procedures to the following: 1 M guanidine HCl and 0.1 M Tris HCl pH 8.0. Further details of the principles of the discontinuous enzymatic assay can be found in prior studies, including the use of DTNB (5,5-dithio-bis-(2-nitrobenzoic acid)) to react with CoA [ 33 , 34 ].
sections.results:
The Ef BltD enzyme catalyzes the bisubstrate reaction that uses AcCoA as a donor and polyamines as the acceptor substrates. While several structures of polyamine acetyltransferases have been reported across different organisms, there is limited knowledge about the diversity of structures of bacterial polyamine acetyltransferases across multiple organisms. We were particularly interested in obtaining a crystal structure of the Ef BltD protein in complex with polyamines since structures of acetyltransferases with polyamines bound in their acceptor sites are also limited in the PDB. In this study, we pre-incubated the Ef BltD protein with AcCoA, CoA, spermine, or spermidine and set up co-crystallization trials to determine whether we could obtain a structure of the Ef BltD protein in complex with any of these ligands. The goal was to learn more about how substrates and/or products bind to this protein. In this study, the Ef BltD protein crystallized in a single condition, which was the same as the apo Ef BltD structure (PDB ID: 2fl4). Numerous co-crystallization and soaking attempts did not yield a crystal structure of the protein in complex with substrates or products. We determined a higher resolution structure and found acetate bound to a region of the protein that was outside of the donor and acceptor sites (PDB ID: 9dsb). Interestingly, the acetate molecule was only found in one protomer of this structure.

The Ef BltD protein crystallized in the P3 space group with two protein molecules in the asymmetric unit (RMSD of 0.3367 Å for 146 common Cα atoms for the two monomers) at 1.50 Å resolution (PDB ID: 9dsb). The monomer adopts the classical Gcn5-related N -acetyltransferase (GNAT) structural fold, but in the dimer the N-terminal domains are swapped ( Fig. 1 ). The subunits are very tightly interlocked with a contact surface area of 3586.3 Å 2 . This dimer is different from other previously structurally characterized dimeric polyamine acetyltransferases. The Ef BltD protein structure contains several α-helices that surround an internal β-sheet. This β-sheet contains a β-bulge that defines the two substrate binding sites for the donor and acceptor molecules. The first β-strand and two α-helices of the N-terminal end of one protomer are located within the second protomer. This swapped β-strand (β1) is added to the N-terminal end of the central β-sheet of the opposite protomer, whereas the two α-helices (α1 and α2) are located at the interface between protomers ( Fig. 1 ).

A comparison of the two Ef BltD crystal structures (PDB IDs: 2fl4, 9dsb) showed a few changes in residue conformations. The most significant conformational change observed between the two structures was for residues W65 and Q66 ( Fig. 2A ). The original Ef BltD structure (PDB ID: 2fl4) was determined at 1.60 Å resolution, has a monomer in the asymmetric unit, was crystallized under identical conditions, but acetate is not present in this structure. The new Ef BltD structure (PDB ID: 9dsb) has a single acetate molecule in one protomer that is bound in a small pocket between W65 and D73. Since the second protomer of this structure does not contain acetate, the protomers are non-equivalent ( Fig. 2A ). When acetate is bound, there is a significant impact on the conformation of nearby residues, which enables a new H-bond to be formed between the E44 sidechain oxygen atom and the Q66 sidechain nitrogen atom. In absence of acetate in the second protomer, the rings of W65 and W71 interact using pi-pi stacking and the Q66 sidechain oxygen atom forms an H-bond with the backbone nitrogen atom of D67. These same interactions are not present in the original Ef BltD structure, and the W65 residue adopts a conformation that is intermediate between the conformations observed for the two protomers of the new structure ( Fig. 2A ). Ultimately, the mode of binding for acetate shows the flexibility of residues in this region of the protein and may provide clues that these residues could alter their conformations upon acceptor substrate binding.

To define the locations of the donor and acceptor sites of the Ef BltD protein, we compared its structure with that of the bacterial polyamine acetyltransferase homolog SpeG since we had structures of this protein in complex with both substrates. The SpeG protein catalyzes the same reaction as the Ef BltD protein and maintains a conserved GNAT structural fold, but it adopts a different oligomeric assembly. We superimposed a single protomer of the SpeG protein crystal structure in complex with N 1 -acetylspermine (PDB ID: 6e1x chain D) onto the Ef BltD protein structure to help identify the approximate location of the acceptor site of the Ef BltD protein. We also superimposed a single protomer of the SpeG protein crystal structure in complex with AcCoA (PDB ID: 4r57 chain A) to identify the approximate location of the donor site. Next, we manually examined the Ef BltD structure to identify residues that correspond to these substrate binding sites ( Fig. 2B ). We found the donor site was primarily comprised of the P-loop (I77-Q84; IDQRFQGQ), the loop between α4 and β5 (Y112–N115; YDTN), and the three residues F75 (β4), L121 (α4), and Y122 (α4). The Y122 residue is in a similar location as other GNAT proteins and typically acts as the general acid, which is required for catalysis in many GNAT proteins. The residues within the donor site will likely exhibit conformational changes in an active conformation of the protein since the N-terminal α2 helix of the swapped protomer occupies a portion of this space. The acceptor site is largely comprised of residues on a flexible loop between β5 and β6 (D134-E138; DTNGE) and residues on different β-strands (β3, β4 and β5) of the central β-sheet that include W65, W71, D73, R74, Y108, and S110. The conformation of Y108 in the current structure is pointed away from the acceptor site and is influenced by the conformation of W65 and W71, but we included it as part of the acceptor site since it may adopt a different conformation in the presence of polyamine ligand.

Our examination of the Ef BltD structure showed residues of the α2-helix occupies portions of both the donor and acceptor sites ( Fig. 3 ). There are several H-bonds that occur between residues that are located on α2 and β4 from opposite protomers and appear to help stabilize the two swapped N-terminal helices of the dimer. These include S31, N35, E38, and R74 ( Fig. 3 region 1). Additionally, the dimer is further stabilized by several interactions between residues of the α2 helix and residues within or near the donor and acceptor site. For example, the residues in the loop between α4 and β5 near the donor site (Y112.B, T114.B, and N115.B) form H-bonds with residues that are located on the swapped α2 helix from the opposite protomer (Q26.A and E30.A) ( Fig. 3 region 2). Q26.A forms an H-bond with the sidechain oxygen atom of T114.B, and E30.A forms an H-bond with the backbone nitrogen atom of Y112.B and an H-bond with the sidechain nitrogen atom of N115.B. Additionally, residues within the acceptor site (W71.B, D73.B, D134.B, N136.B) of the protein form interactions with residues of the swapped α2 helix (A33.A, E34.A, K37.A) ( Fig. 3 region 2). These include an H-bond between K37.A and D134.B, water-mediated H-bonds to E34.A and D73.B, and cation-pi interactions with W71.B. The A33.A residue also forms an H-bond between its backbone oxygen atom and the nitrogen atom of the N136.B sidechain. Based on these interactions, we concluded the N-terminal swapped α2 helix prohibits ligand binding and explains both how the dimer is stabilized and why we were likely unable to obtain a structure with either substrate molecule bound in the crystal. These data support an inhibited state of this protein in the crystal.

Since we found the Ef BltD crystal structure appeared to represent an inhibited form of the protein, the next question we asked was if the protein was catalytically active. To determine whether the protein used for crystallization trials was active, we performed steady-state enzyme kinetics assays. We initially screened this enzyme for activity toward a few compounds, including spermine, spermidine, thialysine, l -lysine, tobramycin, and kanamycin B and found it was only active toward spermine and spermidine ( Supplemental Fig. 2 ). Therefore, we performed substrate saturation curves using AcCoA as the donor and spermine and spermidine as acceptor substrates and determined kinetic parameters for Ef BltD ( Fig. 4 and Table 2 ). We found the Ef BltD protein exhibits significant activity toward these two polyamines, with a higher turnover number (23.7 s −1 vs 0.66 s −1 ) and higher apparent affinity (76.1 μM vs 424 μM) for spermine compared to spermidine ( Table 2 ). The catalytic efficiency of the Ef BltD enzyme was also two orders of magnitude higher for spermine than spermidine, indicating spermine is the preferential substrate. These results were consistent with the parameters previously reported for the Ef BltD enzyme ( Table 2 ) [ 8 ]. During our kinetic characterization and data fitting, we observed positive cooperativity of the Ef BltD enzyme for spermine; no cooperativity was observed when spermidine was the substrate ( Fig. 4 and Table 2 ). The allosteric sigmoidal model was selected over the simpler Michaelis-Menten model of non-linear fitting based on the extra sum-of-squares F test, where the P value was 0.0042 for the spermine substrate saturation curve. It is possible this cooperativity occurs due to the symmetry of the spermine molecule compared to spermidine and the fact that the B. subtilis BltD was previously shown to only acetylate the N 1 position of spermidine, not N 8 [ 19 ]. Thus, spermidine only has one opportunity for acetylation (one aminopropyl group) whereas spermine has two aminopropyl groups and thus two opportunities for acetylation. This is not the first polyamine acetyltransferase, nor GNAT enzyme [ 35 , 36 ], to exhibit positive cooperativity. For example, the bacterial polyamine acetyltransferase homolog SpeG from Vibrio cholerae displays significant positive cooperativity when either spermine or spermidine are substrates [ 37 ]. The Ef BltD enzyme is unique compared to SpeG since cooperativity is only observed for spermine, not spermidine.

Since we found the protein used for crystallization trials was catalytically active but the conformation of the protein in the crystal structure appeared to be an inhibited form, we hypothesized the protein in solution may exist either in a different dimeric form than what was crystallized, or it is a monomer. This hypothesis was partially based on our examination of the Alphafold2 model of the Ef BltD protein, which showed it could theoretically adopt a different conformation of the N-terminal domain that would support an accessible active site and catalytically active enzyme ( Fig. 5 ). Therefore, we performed analytical size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) to determine the oligomeric state of the protein in solution. First, we examined the protein in the absence of substrates and found a single peak that corresponded to a monomer in solution (theoretical monomer 17.7 kDa and experimental monomer 16.9 kDa; Fig. 6 ). Next, we incubated the protein in the presence of different concentrations of AcCoA and/or spermine substrates and then subjected it to SEC. We found the protein elutes as a monomer regardless of the presence of substrates, which indicates they do not influence the oligomeric state of the Ef BltD protein ( Fig. 6 ). The second peak that was observed in all chromatograms where AcCoA was present is likely excess AcCoA since as its concentration increases the intensity of this peak also increases proportionally. To determine whether a higher ordered oligomer could form in solution under conditions that partially mimicked the crystallization conditions, we dialyzed the protein into 50 mM sodium acetate pH 4.5 buffer with either 500 mM or 1 M NaCl and performed SEC after column equilibration. Regardless of the concentration of NaCl, the protein did not shift toward a higher oligomer and instead eluted much later than smaller molecules like AcCoA ( Supplemental Figure 3 , Fig. 6 ). It is possible the protein is adsorbing to the column via hydrophobic interactions since the pI of the protein (5.07) is near the pH of the buffer (4.5). Thus, there is no evidence for formation of a higher ordered oligomer or dynamic equilibrium of different oligomers for the Ef BltD protein in solution in either buffer in these experiments. We therefore conclude the most likely active form of the Ef BltD protein is monomeric.
sections.discussion:
We found the Ef BltD protein is both very active and exhibits a monomeric state in solution. This led us to propose three different scenarios that explain its dimeric state in the crystal:

The first scenario is that the dimeric structure of this protein is an artifact of crystallization. We hypothesize this would be due to the high protein and salt concentration (3 M) and low pH (4.5) in the crystallization condition that favors binding residues of the N-terminally swapped portion of the protein primarily within the acceptor site. Since protein crystals did not grow in any other conditions, it is likely that the monomeric protein, even in the presence of substrates that could theoretically stabilize the conformation of its N-terminus, is not readily crystallizable. This could be due to possible dynamic motions of the protein in solution that do not favor a stable monomeric conformation of the enzyme for crystallization.

The second scenario is that the K37 residue mimics a substructure of a polyamine molecule and is located in a similar position as what would be anticipated for binding this type of substrate within the acceptor site. In theory, the local concentration of the N-terminus that contains this residue, in addition to other residues within the helix, could favor this dimeric form over a structure in complex with polyamine given its random kinetic mechanism for binding substrates. While this lysine residue could indeed mimic a polyamine substructure, the spermine molecule is longer and we would anticipate additional interactions with acidic residues in the acceptor site would be required. In contrast, it could be just a coincidence that a lysine residue is bound in this location and does not predict how a polyamine could bind to this protein. Further experiments probing the importance of this residue will be explored in the near future.

The third scenario is that the dimer represents an inhibited state of the protein that may transition to an active monomeric form during different physiological conditions in the cell. When we examined the predicted oligomeric state of the Ef BltD protein using in silico methodologies via EPPIC [ 42 ] and PISA [ 43 ], we found both of these programs asserted the most stable biological assembly was a homodimer. However, we suspect this computational result could also be biased by the fact that the conformation that is represented in the crystal structure is stabilized by significant interactions between the swapped N-terminal domain and the active site as described above. Additionally, our evaluation of the AlphaFold2 model of the monomeric Ef BltD protein proposes an alternate form may be possible ( Fig. 7A ).

These scenarios lead to the question of whether the dimeric form of the Ef BltD protein that was obtained under acidic conditions could be physiologically relevant. For example, it may be possible that the Ef BltD protein exists in dynamic equilibrium where cellular signals or altered pHs promote different forms of the protein. The interchange between oligomeric states is plausible, but whether it is energetically feasible or not remains in question. Regardless, one could envision a situation where the cell would benefit from the protein being already synthesized and in an inhibited state that could then be activated by binding a small molecule or forming a specific protein-protein interaction. Alternatively, a regulatory mechanism that would involve sensing an increase in pH due to an overabundance of basic polyamine molecules might promote the formation of the more active Ef BltD monomer to acetylate polyamines and maintain intracellular pH. Indeed, biogenic amines are not produced as readily at low pH in E. faecalis [ 44 , 45 ], which could render the dimeric inhibited structure we identified here to be relevant in acidic conditions. This type of dynamic transition between oligomeric states and/or effects on kinetic activity has been noted for other types of proteins [ 46 – 50 ]. While we do not know the answer to this question, we acknowledge an alternative possibility for oligomerization with BltD proteins may exist.

Our comparison of the Ef BltD protein sequence showed relatively high sequence identity to a variety of other Gram-positive human gut bacteria ( Table 3 top; Supplemental Fig. 4 ). When we constricted the sequence comparison of the Ef BltD protein with other Enterococcus species, we found the sequence identity decreased to ~33–40% identity ( Table 3 middle; Supplemental Fig. 5 ). Furthermore, we found the sequence identity between Ef BltD and Bs BltD was ~45% but was considerably lower when compared to the Ef PmvE and Bs PaiA proteins (~20% identity) ( Table 3 bottom; Supplemental Fig. 6 ). The sequence alignments between the BltD proteins from these two organisms showed the Bs BltD protein has an insertion that is not present in the Ef BltD protein (between W65 and Q66 of the Ef BltD protein) ( Supplemental Fig. 6A ). Additionally, when we compared the conservation of donor and acceptor site residues between these BltD proteins we found most residues were conserved or had similar chemical properties. However, we did observe a few residues that more drastically altered their chemical properties. These included (numbers correspond to the Ef BltD protein): Q84K, T114N, and T135F ( Fig. 7 ). Our comparison of the Ef BltD donor and acceptor site residues across the other proteins, either from Gram-positive human gut bacteria or across other Enterococcal species also showed high conservation of these residues ( Supplemental Figs. 4 and 5 ). This same comparison between BltD and PmvE/PaiA proteins showed less conservation of these residues ( Supplemental Fig. 6 ).

Our study provides a glimpse into the first crystal structure of any BltD polyamine acetyltransferase and helps to compliment previous functional studies of BltD homologs. The N-terminal domain swapping observed for the Ef BltD protein structure appears to be unique compared to previously structurally characterized GNAT proteins. To our knowledge, GNATs have only displayed examples of C-terminal domain swapped dimers that form different arrangements of the swapped secondary structures. Therefore, the Ef BltD protein represents a novel structure for the GNAT superfamily. Moreover, the Ef BltD protein structure shows that additional structural diversity in polyamine acetyltransferases exists compared to previous structural studies for these types of enzymes, such as SpeG and PaiA.

Our kinetic characterization of the Ef BltD protein showed this enzyme consistently exhibits a preference for spermine compared to spermidine, which has been observed for several polyamine acetyltransferases that acetylate these polyamines ( Table 2 ). When we compared the Ef BltD kinetic activity to other Gram-positive bacterial polyamine acetyltransferases (SpeG and PaiA/PmvE) we found the Ef BltD enzyme has similar catalytic efficiency for spermine as SpeG enzymes and its catalytic efficiency for spermidine is comparable to the B. subtilis PaiA protein toward spermine ( Table 2 ). The Ef PmvE protein was shown to acetylate spermine and putrescine, but it was not kinetically characterized to determine kinetic parameters that could be used to compare catalytic efficiencies [ 15 ]. However, it is likely that it would exhibit similar activity to other PaiA proteins that have been characterized. If this was indeed the case, the Ef BltD protein could be considered a comparatively more efficient enzyme for spermine than PmvE/PaiA.

Since we know there are at least two GNAT polyamine acetyltransferases in E. faecalis (PmvE and BltD) and only the Ef BltD crystal structure presented in this study has been determined, we compared the Ef BltD AlphaFold2 model to the Ef PmvE homolog B. subtilis PaiA ( Bs PaiA) protein structure (PDB ID: 1tiq). The Bs PaiA protein has also been determined to be monomeric in solution [ 40 ]. We found the Ef BltD and Bs PaiA protein structures show several key alterations between these proteins ( Fig. 7B and C ). These include an N-terminal alpha helical region and a C-terminal β-strand versus loop conformation between the two proteins. When we compared the conservation of acceptor site residues between these proteins, we found two acceptor site residues (R74, G137) and the catalytic Y122 residue were conserved, but most residues in this region of the protein exhibited different chemical properties between the two proteins ( Fig. 7C ). These alterations in conservation of acceptor site residues may explain the differences observed in catalytic efficiency between these two enzymes.

It is not known whether E. faecalis has a SpeG homolog in its genome, but other Enterococcal bacteria appear to have three possible combinations of GNAT polyamine acetyltransferases: SpeG, BltD, and PaiA/PmvE. At present, there does not appear to be a clear pattern to polyamine acetyltransferase gene redundancy within genomes of different organisms. Many bacteria, including Enterococcal species, import polyamines to aid their survival. Therefore, it is expected they would harbor enzymes that are finely tuned to regulate intracellular polyamine concentrations under a variety of conditions. Since bacteria encounter different polyamines in their everyday environments, such as in the gut microbiome of different organisms, it is possible these enzymes are differentially expressed. Further study is required to elucidate the cellular states in which these enzymes would be catalytically active. Furthermore, the questions of why redundant polyamine acetyltransferase enzymes are encoded within bacterial genomes and when the different types of enzymes are transcribed and utilized in the cell remain outstanding. Due to significant structural divergence between the different types of polyamine acetyltransferases, it may be a viable strategy to design selective inhibitors that target one type of polyamine acetyltransferase over others. For example, if the dimeric state of the Ef BltD protein is non-physiologically relevant, then the manner in which the protein interacts with the swapped peptide within its acceptor site could potentially be utilized to design BltD-specific inhibitors.
sections.conclusion: This study has provided insight into the structure/function relationship of the Ef BltD protein and how it compares and contrasts with other polyamine acetyltransferases from different organisms. While several polyamine acetyltransferases exist within different organisms, the BltD protein is unique due to its substantial preference for spermine over spermidine and its X-ray crystal structure that showed N-terminal domain swapping. We performed multiple crystallization trials to obtain a liganded complex of this protein with substrates and/or products, but we were unsuccessful. Our detailed analysis of the crystal structure, enzyme kinetics, and oligomeric state led to the hypothesis that the crystallized form of the protein represented an inhibited state. We propose this structure will be useful for designing targeted inhibitors for this protein. Additionally, we show that the N-terminus of this protein is flexible and the Ef BltD crystal structure is novel for the GNAT superfamily of proteins.
